quote: Alle ein-eindeutige Transformationen im Raume beliebiger Dimension finden
english: Find all one-to-one transformations in space of arbitrary dimension
topic: Notes on invariant theory: determining which functions are entire, finding systems of ternary linear forms analogous to Gordan's systems of quadratic forms, finding all one-to-one transformations of space, applying the transfer process to a covariant expression, and a remark that even infinitely many forms have a finite system of invariants.

triage.modern_statement: This is most likely a request to describe the Cremona group Bir(P^n) for every n. That is the group of birational self-maps of n-dimensional projective space (what 19th-century geometers called 'ein-eindeutige' or one-to-one rational transformations). Concretely, the task is to find generators for this group, and ideally a full classification or presentation. The note is very short, so this reading is a likely interpretation, not a certain one. Read literally, it could also mean bijections or homeomorphisms, but in that sense the question would be trivial or meaningless.
triage.answered_by: Partly answered. For n=2, Noether stated a generation theorem in the 1870s and Castelnuovo proved it in 1901: Bir(P^2) over an algebraically closed field is generated by PGL_3 and the standard quadratic involution. A later presentation by generators and relations is due to Blanc and others (arXiv 1802.02735; Proc. AMS 2019). For n>=3, Hudson (1927) and Pan (1999) showed that Bir(P^n) cannot be generated by elements of bounded degree. Blanc, Lamy and Zimmermann proved that over subfields of C it is not simple and is not generated by linear and Jonquières maps. No explicit generating set is known for n>=3. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Noether–Castelnuovo theorem (Castelnuovo 1901): the plane Cremona group Bir(P^2) has explicit generators; a presentation using these generators was later given.
Hudson and Pan: for n>=3, Bir(P^n) is not generated by Aut(P^n) plus finitely many elements, or by any set of bounded degree. No explicit list of generators is known for n>=3.

Cantat's survey: Cr2(k) is not finitely generated; the Hudson–Pan theorem says generating Cr_n(k) for n>=3 needs as many algebraic families of generators as there are families of (n-2)-dimensional varieties.
For n>=3, Cremona groups are much less well understood, and any generating set must be complicated.
Blanc–Lamy–Zimmermann: Cr_n is not simple for n>=3 and is not generated by linear and Jonquières elements.

triage.why: In 19th-century German usage, 'ein-eindeutige Transformationen' in the context of invariant theory usually meant birational (Cremona) transformations, so I take the note to ask for all Cremona transformations in every dimension. The plane case was settled by Castelnuovo in 1901, building on Noether. In dimension 3 and higher, no explicit description is known, and only negative or structural results exist (Hudson, Pan, Blanc–Lamy–Zimmermann). Recent papers show the field is still active. Confidence is only medium because the note is short and I am inferring the birational reading from period usage and context, not from anything else on the page.
